HIST 270 · Chapter 5 · Lecture 2

Early Tang Power

From the Saddle to the Mirror: winning an empire, then keeping it

One reign, six places · 617–676

Historical photograph · Six Steeds of Zhaoling (636–649), Beilin Museum, Xi’an · Photo: Bairuilong, CC BY-SA 4.0

Welcome to Lecture 2 of Chapter 5. Last time you watched the Sui reunite China and then break itself. This lecture follows the family that picked up the pieces: Li Yuan, who founded the Tang in 618, and his son Li Shimin, who became Emperor Taizong.

Look at the photograph. These are real stone reliefs, not an AI image. They show six warhorses that Taizong rode in the civil wars, carved for his tomb. The next slide looks closely at one of them. They are the emperor’s own choice of how to be remembered: on horseback, winning.

Keep one sentence in mind for the whole lecture: swords won the Tang its empire; cooperation kept it, and where victory could not be turned into cooperation, Tang power stopped.

Use the S key to open these notes and click dotted words for short explanations. The self-check slides let you test yourself before you look at the answers.

Check yourself: What does it suggest about Taizong that he wanted horses, not law codes or palaces, carved at his tomb?

Zhaoling · Taizong’s tomb, carved 636–649

An emperor chose to be remembered by his warhorses.

The order: Taizong had six of his civil-war horses carved in stone for his tomb.
621: near Luoyang, an arrow struck Saluzi in the chest.
The scene: General Qiu Xinggong pulls the arrow out. Loyalty, not slaughter.
The monument remembers the battles. It leaves out how he took the throne, and where he failed.

Sources: Penn Museum, object C395, and museum object history; Denis Twitchett, ed., Cambridge History of China, vol. 3.

This slide opens the story with an object the emperor designed for himself. Late in his reign, Taizong ordered six stone reliefs of horses he had ridden in the wars that founded the Tang. They were set up at his tomb, Zhaoling, on a mountain northwest of Chang’an. Two of the six, including this one, are now at the Penn Museum in Philadelphia; the other four are in Xi’an.

Look at the relief. Saluzi, or “Autumn Dew,” was hit by an arrow during the fighting near Luoyang in 621. General Qiu Xinggong is shown pulling it out. The sculptor did not show an enemy being killed. He showed care, courage, and loyal service. The relief was made years after the battle, so it is not a record of what the scene looked like. It is a designed monument with a political purpose.

Why this matters: the monument tells you how Taizong wanted his rise remembered. Your job in this lecture is to learn the rest of the story, including the parts the tomb leaves out. We will come back to this tomb at the very end.

Check yourself: What can this relief reliably tell you about 621, and what can it tell you more directly about Taizong’s later image?

The journey ahead

One reign, six places: how a conqueror became a ruler.

1 · 617–628The SaddleWinning the civil wars
2 · 626The GateTaking the throne by force
3 · 626The BridgeFacing the Türks at the capital
4 · 620s–640sThe MirrorLearning to rule: court and village
5 · 630The SteppeBecoming Heavenly Qaghan
6 · 645The FortressFinding the limit at Ansi
The thread: swords won the Tang its empire; cooperation kept it. Where victory could not be turned into cooperation, Tang power stopped.

Sources: Cambridge History of China, vol. 3; Howard J. Wechsler, Mirror to the Son of Heaven; Shao-yun Yang, Early Tang China and the World.

This slide is your map of the lecture. Instead of acts, the story moves through six places in the life of Li Shimin, the man who became Emperor Taizong. The places run roughly in order, though the Mirror years (his court and the villages it governed) overlap with the steppe victory of 630.

The Saddle is the civil war that won China. The Gate is the palace gate where he killed his brothers. The Bridge is the river crossing where a Türk army nearly reached his capital weeks later. The Mirror is his court, where he kept a critic close, and the villages where the state counted families. The Steppe is the grassland north of China, where he became a steppe ruler as well as an emperor. The Fortress is Ansi in Korea, where his armies could not win. A short coda follows his son’s wars in Korea.

By the end, you should be able to explain how the founding and the 626 coup mixed continuity with violence, connect registration, land, taxes, soldiers, law, and recruitment, and compare the Tang’s success on the steppe with its limits in Korea.

Check yourself: Which of the six places do you predict will show the limit of Tang power, and why?

Li Shimin’s cavalry before Luoyang, 621

Place 1 · The Saddle · 617–628

Winning the Empire

The father proclaimed a dynasty. The son won it on horseback.

AI-generated historical interpretation · Tang tomb-mural style

The first place is the saddle. When the Sui collapsed, many men tried to found the next dynasty. Li Yuan, a Sui governor in the north, was one of them. His second son, Li Shimin, became the family’s best general, and his victories gave the Tang its territory and gave Li Shimin himself enormous prestige.

Look at the image. It is an AI-generated historical interpretation in the Tang tomb-mural style. It is not evidence. It imagines Li Shimin in lamellar armor on a dark horse, leading his cavalry and their red banners past the walls and gate towers of Luoyang, the city he besieged in 620–621. Note what it leaves out: no defeated rivals, no burned towns. Victory pictures show the winners; the cost for everyone else is in the text.

Why this matters: the Tang began as one armed faction among many. Everything later in the story, including Li Shimin’s claim to the throne, grew out of the power he built in these wars.

Check yourself: Why might the most successful general in a founding war become a danger to his own family?

Founding the dynasty · 617–618

The Tang founders came from the same northwestern ruling world as the Sui.

Li Yuan: a Sui governor at Taiyuan and part of the Guanlong elite.
Family: his mother and Sui Wendi’s empress were sisters.
617: he rose in revolt, took Chang’an, and set up a puppet Sui prince.
618: after Yangdi’s murder, he removed the prince and proclaimed the Tang.
A new dynasty took over an existing capital, ruling class, and set of institutions.

Sources: Denis Twitchett, ed., Cambridge History of China, vol. 3; David A. Graff, Medieval Chinese Warfare; Digital Dunhuang, Cave 220.

×

Guanlong elite

A network of military families rooted around the passes (guan) near Chang’an and the Long region to the west. Many had served the Western Wei, Northern Zhou, and Sui. “Elite” here means families with offices, land, marriage connections, and military commands, not a single ethnic group or a modern political party.

This slide shows that the Tang founders were insiders, not outsiders. Li Yuan had served the Sui as governor at Taiyuan in the north. His family belonged to the Guanlong elite, a network of military and officeholding families centered on the Chang’an region and the northwest. These families had served the Northern Zhou and the Sui and were tied together by marriage. Li Yuan’s mother and Sui Wendi’s empress were sisters, so the Tang and Sui ruling houses were close relatives. Click the dotted term for a fuller definition.

In 617 Li Yuan rose in revolt, seized Chang’an, and placed a young Sui prince on the throne as a puppet. In 618, after Yangdi was murdered at Jiangdu (the final scene of the last lecture), Li Yuan removed the prince and declared the Tang. He is known as Emperor Gaozu.

Look at the mural. It dates from 642 and shows an imperial figure in a Buddhist story. It is traditionally identified as Taizong, but it was not painted to record his appearance. Read it as evidence for how early Tang artists pictured imperial authority surrounded by officials.

Check yourself: What two kinds of continuity helped the Tang founders take over the Sui state quickly?

Consolidation · 618–628

Founding the Tang in 618 did not mean controlling China in 618.

618Li Yuan becomes Emperor Gaozu at Chang’an. Rival regimes hold most of the old Sui empire.
621Li Shimin defeats Wang Shichong and Dou Jiande near Luoyang.
624Major southern rivals are defeated.
628The last major holdout, Liang Shidu, falls.
The Tang was founded by proclamation, but reunification took another decade of war and bargaining.

Independent study: how Li Shimin won the civil wars, 618–628 →

Sources: David A. Graff, Medieval Chinese Warfare; Cambridge History of China, vol. 3.

This slide moves fast on purpose. A dynasty can announce its beginning in a day, but it cannot make rivals disappear by announcement. When Gaozu founded the Tang in 618, other warlords controlled much of the former Sui empire. Li Shimin became the dynasty’s most important commander. In 621 he defeated two major rivals, Wang Shichong and Dou Jiande, in the struggle for Luoyang and the eastern plain. By 624 most large southern rivals had fallen, but Liang Shidu held out in the north until 628.

This corrects a common shortcut: “the Tang reunified China in 618.” The year 618 marks the dynasty’s founding, not the end of the conquest. Tang victory also depended on absorbing surrendered soldiers and officials and confirming local leaders, turning former enemies into servants of the new court. That pattern returns on the steppe after 630.

If you want the full story of the 621 campaign, follow the independent-study link to the Pierian Spring section at the end of the deck.

Why this matters: a capital, a dynastic name, and an emperor are not the same as effective rule across an empire.

Check yourself: Why is 628 a better end date for Tang military consolidation than 618?

Xuanwu Gate at dawn, 626

Place 2 · The Gate · 626

Taking the Throne

The empire’s best general was not its heir.

AI-generated historical interpretation · Tang tomb-mural style

The second place is a gate. By 626 Li Shimin had won the wars, commanded loyal officers, and earned a huge reputation. But he was Gaozu’s second son. The heir was his older brother, Li Jiancheng, the crown prince. A crown prince is the son officially chosen to inherit the throne.

Look at the image. It is an AI-generated interpretation, not a surviving picture. It imagines the morning of the ambush at Xuanwu Gate, the northern gate of the palace in Chang’an. We stand in the dark gate passage with Li Shimin’s armored archers, who wait in the shadows on both sides. Through the arch, two princes in court robes, one in green on a brown horse and one in red on a white horse, ride toward the gate: think of them as Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji, unaware of the trap. The violence that follows is implied, not shown.

One caution about the picture: the palace hall behind the princes is the artist’s interpretation. Its stacked, upturned roofs look more like later imperial palaces, such as Beijing’s Ming-era Forbidden City, than the broader, simpler halls of Tang Chang’an.

Notice the contrast with the warhorse relief at the start of the lecture. The tomb remembered loyalty on the battlefield. This gate is where loyalty inside the family broke.

Why this matters: the Tang’s most admired reign began with a killing. You need both facts in view to judge Taizong fairly.

Check yourself: What is a crown prince, and why did Li Shimin’s military success make the succession dangerous?

Xuanwu Gate · 2 July 626

Li Shimin ambushed his brothers and forced his father aside.

Rivalry: Crown Prince Li Jiancheng and brother Li Yuanji feared Shimin’s power and followers.
2 July 626: Shimin’s men ambushed both brothers at Xuanwu Gate. Both were killed.
Afterward: the brothers’ sons were executed; Shimin was named heir.
4 Sept. 626: Gaozu abdicated. Li Shimin became Emperor Taizong.
The celebrated “Reign of Good Government” began with political murder.

Abdicate: to give up the throne. Zhenguan (627–649): Taizong’s reign name, later remembered as a model “Reign of Good Government.”

Sources: Cambridge History of China, vol. 3; Howard J. Wechsler, Mirror to the Son of Heaven.

This slide tells what happened at the gate. Military success made Li Shimin powerful, but it did not make him heir. Competition between his followers and those of Crown Prince Li Jiancheng and a younger brother, Li Yuanji, became dangerous. On 2 July 626, Li Shimin and his men ambushed both brothers at Xuanwu Gate, the northern gate of the palace. Both were killed. Their sons were then executed, removing rivals from the next generation. Li Shimin became crown prince, and about two months later Gaozu abdicated.

Read the record critically. The court histories were compiled under Taizong and his successors, and they had strong reasons to justify him. They often portray Li Jiancheng as dangerous or unworthy and Li Shimin as the dynasty’s necessary savior. Historians separate the basic events from the moral explanation offered by sources written for the winner.

Look at the portrait. It was painted in the Ming dynasty, roughly 700 years later. It shows how later artists imagined a model emperor, not what Li Shimin looked like.

Check yourself: How does the Xuanwu Gate coup complicate the image created by the Saluzi relief?

Place 3 · The Bridge · Wei River, September 626

Weeks after the coup, a Türk army camped across the river from the capital.

The threat: Illig Qaghan’s cavalry reached the Wei River, a short ride from Chang’an.
The gamble: Taizong rode to the bank with a small escort and spoke across the water.
The price: a truce sealed at the Bian Bridge, and valuables to send the Türks home.
The new emperor could kill his brothers. He could not yet defend his capital by force.

Türks: a Turkic-speaking empire of the Mongolian steppe. Qaghan: its supreme ruler.

Sources: Sima Guang, Zizhi tongjian, ch. 191; Jonathan Karam Skaff, Sui-Tang China and Its Turko-Mongol Neighbors; Shao-yun Yang, Early Tang China and the World.

This slide shows how fragile the new emperor was. Only weeks after the Xuanwu Gate coup, the Eastern Türk ruler Illig Qaghan led a large cavalry army to the Wei River near Chang’an. The Türks were a Turkic-speaking steppe empire; a qaghan was their supreme ruler, a stronger title than the familiar word “khan.”

According to the traditional account, Taizong rode out to the riverbank with a small escort and spoke to the qaghan across the water. Days later the two sides sealed a truce at the Bian Bridge, and the Tang sent valuables to secure the Türk withdrawal. Relations were already tangled: Gaozu had sought Türk help during the civil wars, so the Tang depended on the Türks as well as fearing them.

Look at the image. It is an AI-generated interpretation in the Tang tomb-mural style, not a record of the scene. It stages the contrast in the traditional account. On the near bank, Taizong in yellow sits on a white horse with only a few attendants. Across the water, a vast Türk cavalry army fills the far bank, with felt tents and horse herds behind it. Between them runs a long timber bridge, standing in for the Bian Bridge where the bargain was made.

Read the key under the picture. It labels the sides: the Türks camped on the north bank, and Taizong came out from Chang’an, a short ride south of the river. The picture also compresses time: Taizong’s ride to the riverbank and the truce on the bridge were days apart.

Why this matters: hold on to this low point. Four years later, the story on the steppe will look completely different.

Check yourself: Why did the Wei River crisis show that Taizong’s position was still weak in 626?

Check yourself · on your own

Can you explain how the Tang took power?

Answer from memory, in a sentence or two each:

  1. Why is 628, not 618, a better end date for the Tang conquest of China?
  2. Which statement best explains early Tang continuity?
    1. The Tang rejected Sui officials and institutions to begin again.
    2. The Tang inherited elite networks and state structures, then consolidated them through war and political choices.
    3. The Tang controlled all of China as soon as Gaozu declared the dynasty in 618.
    4. Taizong’s good reputation proves that the 626 succession was peaceful.
  3. What did the Wei River crisis reveal about Taizong’s position in 626?

When you have written your answers, compare them with these possible answers.

×

Possible answers

  1. 618 is when Gaozu proclaimed the dynasty, but rival regimes held much of China. Li Shimin’s 621 victories, the fall of southern rivals by 624, and the defeat of Liang Shidu in 628 completed the conquest.
  2. B. The founders came from the Sui governing world and inherited its capital and institutions, but still needed about a decade of war, and the 626 coup, to secure power. A is wrong because the Tang used earlier institutions; C confuses a proclamation with effective rule; D turns a later reputation into a false account of how Taizong took power.
  3. He had won the throne by force inside the palace, but he could not yet defeat the Türks. He had to negotiate and pay to make them withdraw.

Study tip: when a claim uses words such as “all,” “immediately,” or “proves,” check whether it erases a complicated process.

Pause here and answer from memory before you open the possible answers. Trying to recall something and then checking helps you remember it far better than rereading does.

Tips for question 1: look back at the consolidation timeline. Separate the day a dynasty is declared from the years it takes to defeat rivals.

Tips for question 2: the best answer keeps two things in view at once: continuity (Li Yuan was a Sui governor; the Li and Yang houses were related; the Tang kept Chang’an and Sui institutions) and coercion (a decade of war and the killing of Li Shimin’s brothers and their sons). Watch for answers that use absolute words like “all,” “immediately,” or “proves.”

Tips for question 3: compare the gate and the bridge. One shows power inside the palace; the other shows weakness on the frontier.

When you check your answers, look for what you left out, then go back to that slide.

Check yourself: Give one example of continuity and one example of coercion in the Tang’s rise to power.

Place 4 · The Mirror · Taizong’s court, 627–643

Taizong kept the adviser who had urged his brother to strike first.

Before 626: Wei Zheng served Crown Prince Li Jiancheng and reportedly urged him to act against Shimin.
After the coup: Taizong spared him and brought him into the government.
At court: Wei became famous for remonstrance, telling the emperor to his face that he was wrong.
A rival’s adviser became the emperor’s most famous critic.

Sources: Howard J. Wechsler, Mirror to the Son of Heaven: Wei Cheng at the Court of T’ang T’ai-tsung; Cambridge History of China, vol. 3.

The fourth place is a mirror, and it begins with a person. Wei Zheng had served Crown Prince Li Jiancheng and had reportedly urged him to move against Li Shimin before Li Shimin moved first. After the coup, Taizong could have executed him. Instead he brought Wei into the new government.

Wei became famous for remonstrance: formally telling a ruler that a decision is wrong. He criticized the emperor’s spending, temper, and plans, sometimes bluntly. Taizong did not always accept the criticism. He sometimes rejected advice or grew angry. But keeping a former enemy’s adviser close sent a message to officials who had served the losing side: the new emperor wanted their talent and their honesty, not just their silence.

Look at the portrait. It comes from a book printed in 1669, based on the tradition of the portraits of meritorious officials that Taizong had painted in the Lingyan Pavilion in 643. It is an imagined likeness.

Why this matters: this is the first kind of cooperation in our thread: winning over people who had been on the other side.

Check yourself: Why might accepting a former rival’s adviser strengthen a ruler after a violent coup?

Primary source · Taizong on Wei Zheng’s death, 643

What did Taizong say he lost when Wei Zheng died?

Read closely, on your own:

  1. What does each of the three mirrors let a ruler see?
  2. Why might an emperor who took the throne by force want to be remembered as a man who listened to critics?

Bronze mirror: Tang mirrors were polished bronze discs, not glass. Rise and decline: the pattern of dynasties gaining and losing power.

This primary source lets you hear Taizong himself. When Wei Zheng died in 643, Taizong used this “three mirrors” comparison.

How to read it: a bronze mirror shows outward appearance. History shows patterns of rise and decline. An honest person shows a ruler his current mistakes. The statement praises criticism, but it also presents Taizong as an emperor wise enough to accept it. The surviving account comes from the Old Book of Tang, compiled in the tenth century from earlier court records. It preserves an influential court memory, not a recording.

The context: the ideal was not always followed. Within months of Wei’s death, Taizong, angered by reports about Wei’s conduct, had the memorial stone he had written for Wei’s tomb knocked down. Remember that stone. You will see it again at the fortress of Ansi.

Why this matters: the “mirror” is the lecture’s symbol for cooperation inside the court: a ruler needs people who will tell him what power hides.

Check yourself: Why should you read this quotation as an ideal of government rather than proof of how Taizong always behaved?

The Mirror · a county office and a farm, 620s–640s

In a county register, each household became names, ages, and debts to the state.

Register: clerks recorded each household’s members, ages, and legal status.
Land: eligible people received use of state land under equal-field rules.
Taxes: grain (zu), labor (yong, often paid in cloth), and cloth (diao).
Gaps: powerful families hid dependents; people fled the rolls; the south was harder to count.
Registration did not simply count people. It made households visible for taxes and service.

Sources: Wang Binghua and Helen Wang, “Tang Dynasty Tax Textiles”; Valerie Hansen, The Open Empire; Cambridge History of China, vol. 3.

×

Equal-field land and the grain–labor–cloth tax

PartPlain-language meaningConnection to the state
Equal-fieldEligible registered people received use of specified state lands; rules varied by age, status, and region.Land assignments tied farming to registration.
ZuAnnual grain payment.Fed the court, officials, and armies.
YongLabor service, often replaced by a cloth payment.Supplied work or a substitute payment.
DiaoTextile or other local-product payment.Moved portable value to the state.

“Equal-field” does not mean every acre was repeatedly divided into equal private farms. Some land returned to the state when the holder died or grew too old; other land stayed with the household. Private estates also existed.

This slide moves from the court to a farm, where the state met ordinary people. Local officials tried to record who belonged to each household, with age, sex, and legal status. Those records decided who could receive state land assignments and who owed grain, cloth, labor, or military service. Registers were tools that connected households to the state’s demands.

The equal-field system assigned the use of land according to rules based on registered people, age, and status. The tax system is often called zu-yong-diao: zu was grain, yong was labor service that could be replaced with cloth, and diao was textiles or another local product. These duties fell mainly on registered adult men, but the cloth came from women’s household weaving. Click the dotted term for a table.

The system worked imperfectly. Powerful families hid dependents, people fled the rolls, and the rules were hardest to apply in parts of the south. Census totals measure registered people, not everyone.

Look at the image. It is an AI interpretation, not evidence. An official in a green robe and black futou cap sits on a mat in a farmyard while a clerk writes on a scroll. Under Taizong’s dress rules of 630, green marked officials of the sixth and seventh ranks, the level of county magistrates. The family brings what the state wanted: a basket of grain and lengths of silk, while a woman works at the loom beside their thatched mud-brick house. Registration happened household by household, face to face, and every name, age, and field written down became a tax and labor obligation. Notice that the cloth is women’s work; the tax system depended on it.

Check yourself: If a household disappeared from the register, which three kinds of resources might the state lose?

The Mirror · a farmer’s season of service

A farmer could serve as a soldier for a season, then go home to his fields.

At home: selected men farmed and trained in designated districts.
On rotation: units took short turns guarding the capital.
On campaign: they joined temporary armies, then went home when the war ended.
The deal: tax exemptions in return for service, often with their own gear and food.
The fubing were concentrated in the northwest, and they were never the Tang’s only soldiers.

Source: David A. Graff, “The Reach of the Military: Tang,” Journal of Chinese History 1 (2017).

This slide follows one farmer into the army. The fubing system (often translated “garrison militia”) organized part-time soldiers through several hundred local regimental headquarters. Men were selected partly for strength, household resources, and the number of adult males in the family. At home they farmed and trained. Units took turns guarding the capital. In wartime the court formed an expeditionary army under an appointed general; when the campaign ended, soldiers and commander were supposed to go home. In exchange for full or partial tax exemptions, fubing usually supplied much of their own equipment and food.

Two cautions. Regiments were spread very unevenly: most were around Chang’an and across the northwest, reflecting the dynasty’s origins. And the Tang also used conscripts, frontier troops, professional guards, and many allied steppe soldiers.

Look at the image. It is an AI interpretation, not evidence. In a millet field, a farmer in a headwrap hands his plow to his wife and keeps a spear for himself, while a column of armored soldiers in rounded helmets marches down the road away from the village. That handoff is the fubing bargain: when a man left on rotation or campaign, his household had to keep the farm running without him. Fubing soldiers were farmers in uniform for part of the year.

Why this matters: fubing kept armies cheap and kept generals from building private forces, but it depended on short wars. Long, distant campaigns would strain it.

Check yourself: Why did the fubing system work better for temporary campaigns than for permanent distant garrisons?

The Mirror · laws, examinations, and books

The court wrote down its rules and trained the men who would apply them.

Law

The Tang Code: issued 624, revised 637, with an official commentary in 653. The earliest Chinese penal code preserved in full.

Independent study: the Tang Code →

Examinations

Schools and exams such as mingjing and jinshi opened a route into office, but not an equal one.

Independent study: schools and exams →

Texts

An approved commentary on the Confucian classics and official histories of earlier dynasties gave officials a shared reference.

Independent study: standard texts →

Codes, registers, and approved texts let the court coordinate officials who served far from the emperor.

Sources: Wallace Johnson, trans., The T’ang Code; Cambridge History of China, vols. 3 and 5; Chen et al., The Political Economy of China’s Imperial Examination System (2025).

This slide covers three tools of government quickly; each has a full slide in the independent-study section if you want more.

Law. Gaozu’s government issued a Tang code in 624, and Taizong’s court revised it in 637. An authoritative commentary followed in 653 under Gaozong. It is the earliest Chinese penal code preserved as a complete system. That does not mean earlier dynasties lacked written law.

Examinations. Government schools and examinations such as mingjing (knowledge of the Confucian classics) and jinshi (literary composition and policy questions) gave the court another way to find talent. But family privilege and recommendations still filled many posts. You will meet this elite in the next lecture.

Texts. Taizong’s court sponsored the Correct Meaning of the Five Classics under the scholar Kong Yingda, and compiled official histories of recent dynasties, which explained why dynasties rose and fell. That is the “past as a mirror” at work.

Why this matters: a big empire needs shared rules and shared training so that officials far from the emperor act alike.

Check yourself: Why is “the Tang chose officials by examinations” true but incomplete?

Check yourself · on your own

Can you trace how a household became the state’s grain, cloth, and soldiers?

Answer from memory:

  1. Which sequence best explains how the early Tang turned households into state resources?
    1. Examinations → frontier conquest → household registration → land
    2. Household registration → land and duty assignments → taxes, labor, and eligible soldiers
    3. Law code → equal wealth → universal military service
    4. Fubing service → automatic examination success → official office
  2. Name one point where that chain could break down, and the resource the court would lose.
  3. Why did the fubing system suit short campaigns better than long, distant wars?

When you have written your answers, compare them with these possible answers.

×

Possible answers

  1. B. Registers identified households and eligible people; officials then applied rules for land and obligations, producing grain, cloth, labor, and military manpower. A starts with exams, which recruited only a few officials; C is wrong because the code did not make wealth equal and service was not universal; D invents a link that did not exist.
  2. Examples: a powerful family hides dependents (lost taxes and labor); a family flees the rolls (lost grain, cloth, and a possible soldier); officials fail to update registers (land and duties assigned wrongly).
  3. Fubing were farmers. Short campaigns let them return to their fields; long garrison duty far away took them from farms and households that supported them.

Pause and answer from memory before opening the possible answers.

Tips for question 1: look back at the county-register slide. Ask what had to come first: the state could not assign land, taxes, or military duty to people it had not recorded. The chain did not work perfectly and was not equally strong everywhere, but this is how it was designed to fit together.

Tips for question 2: the register slide lists the main gaps in red.

Tips for question 3: the fubing slide describes the deal soldiers made and where they lived.

Study tip: when you see an institutional question, draw arrows and label what moves along them: information, land, grain, cloth, labor, or people. A drawn system is easier to remember than separate definitions.

Check yourself: Without looking, draw the chain from register to soldier and label each arrow.

Li Jing’s winter raid on the Türk camp, 630

Place 5 · The Steppe · 630

Heavenly Qaghan

Four years after the bridge, the qaghan who had threatened Chang’an was Taizong’s prisoner.

AI-generated historical interpretation · Tang tomb-mural style

The fifth place is the steppe, the grassland north of China where the Türks grazed their herds. Remember the Wei River in 626: a new emperor bargaining from weakness. By 630 the situation had flipped.

Look at the image. It is an AI-generated interpretation, not a surviving image. It imagines the surprise winter campaign of 630, when Tang cavalry under General Li Jing rode through snow to strike the Türk camp. Horsemen with red pennants charge toward the white felt yurts, and Türks with braided hair run from their tents. The point is speed and weather: the Tang struck in the season when steppe herds and riders were weakest, and caught the camp unprepared.

As you go through the next slides, watch for two kinds of power. One is military: armies, raids, and captured rulers. The other is relational: alliances with steppe leaders, titles, and the chiefs who agreed to serve. The court could order a registered household to pay grain. It could not simply order a distant steppe ruler to obey. Out here, power depended on negotiation and changing alliances.

Check yourself: What had changed between 626 and 630 that made a Tang victory on the steppe possible? Make a prediction before the next slide.

The Steppe · 627–630

Bad winters, revolts, and a surprise raid broke the Eastern Türk qaghanate.

627–629: harsh winters, revolts by subject peoples, and rival coalitions weakened Illig Qaghan.
Tang move: Taizong allied with discontented steppe leaders, such as the Xueyantuo.
630: Li Jing’s surprise winter campaign shattered Illig’s camp. The qaghan was captured and brought to Chang’an.
The Tang won by entering a steppe crisis, not by defeating an isolated army.

Sources: Shao-yun Yang, Early Tang China and the World; Skaff, Sui-Tang China and Its Turko-Mongol Neighbors.

This slide explains how the steppe story turned. Between 627 and 629, the Eastern Türk qaghanate suffered severe weather that killed livestock, revolts by peoples it had ruled, and challenges from rival coalitions such as the Xueyantuo. For a herding empire, dead animals meant hunger and lost power. Taizong’s court built alliances with dissatisfied steppe leaders. In early 630, General Li Jing led a surprise winter campaign that shattered Illig Qaghan’s camp. Illig was captured soon after and brought to Chang’an, where he lived as a captive until his death a few years later.

Look at the portrait. Like Wei Zheng’s, it comes from a book printed in 1669. It is an imagined likeness.

Why this matters: the jump from weakness in 626 to victory in 630 invites a simple story of Taizong’s genius. A better explanation combines leadership with timing, environmental pressure, and steppe politics. The Tang won by joining an existing struggle and building alliances, as well as by fighting.

Check yourself: Name one Tang factor and one steppe factor that helped produce the victory of 630.

The Steppe · Chang’an, 630

Steppe rulers hailed Taizong as their Heavenly Qaghan.

Spring 630: chiefs and envoys asked Taizong to accept the title Heavenly Qaghan.
Two titles: Son of Heaven to his Chinese subjects; supreme qaghan to steppe peoples.
Real use: he confirmed successors of steppe rulers and issued orders under both titles.
One ruler could speak in more than one political language.

Sources: Shao-yun Yang, Early Tang China and the World, 618–750 CE (Cambridge, 2026), introduction; Skaff, Sui-Tang China and Its Turko-Mongol Neighbors.

×

Heavenly Qaghan · tian kehan

Qaghan was a supreme steppe ruler’s title, stronger than the ordinary English “khan.” In 630, rulers and envoys asked Taizong to accept the hybrid title tian kehan, often translated “Heavenly” or “Celestial Qaghan.” It claimed leadership over peoples once subordinate to the Eastern and Western Türk qaghans; it did not make every steppe community directly administered Tang territory.

This slide shows Taizong taking on a second identity. After the victory of 630, assembled rulers and envoys asked him to accept the title Heavenly Qaghan, or tian kehan. “Heavenly” may echo the steppe sky god, Tengri, while also sounding like the Chinese emperor’s title “Son of Heaven.” The result was a title that made sense in two political traditions at once. Click the dotted term for more.

The title did not turn all of Inner Asia into counties governed like the land around Chang’an. It meant that many rulers who had belonged to the Türk political world now recognized Taizong’s superior status. He could confirm a local ruler’s successor and issue commands under both titles. That recognition lasted only as long as the power and relationships behind it.

Look at the image. It is an AI interpretation, not a record of a specific ceremony. Taizong in yellow sits on a raised dais before a red-columned hall. On the left, Tang officials in red and green robes stand holding court tablets; on the right, Türk chiefs in fur-trimmed robes, with braided hair, kneel while their horses are led forward as gifts. The picture puts both of Taizong’s audiences in one courtyard, which is the point of the double title. Horses were the steppe’s great wealth, and presenting them was how chiefs showed loyalty to a new overlord.

Why this matters: Taizong did not have to choose between being “Chinese” or “steppe.” His court claimed both forms of authority when each was useful.

Check yourself: Why is “Heavenly Qaghan” more informative than translating Taizong’s title simply as “Great Khan”?

The Steppe · after 630

The Tang ruled many Türk communities through their own chiefs.

Submission: more than 100,000 Eastern Türk people accepted Tang authority.
Debate: settle them inside the frontier, push them beyond the Yellow River, or break them up?
Answer: resettlement in the Ordos and bridle prefectures: chiefs took Tang offices but kept leading their people.
Payoff: Türk cavalry fought in Tang armies under their own leaders.
Indirect rule extended Tang reach cheaply, but only while both sides gained from it.

Independent study: the frontier toolkit (fight, negotiate, incorporate) →

Sources: David A. Graff, “The Reach of the Military: Tang”; Skaff, Sui-Tang China and Its Turko-Mongol Neighbors.

×

“Bridle” prefectures · jimi zhou

The Tang gave existing chiefs Chinese-style titles such as prefect or governor-general. They continued leading their own communities and could supply troops to Tang campaigns. The metaphor of a loose bridle suggests guidance without the close control used in an ordinary prefecture.

This slide answers a hard question: what should the Tang do with the people who had followed the defeated qaghan? More than 100,000 submitted. Court officials debated whether to settle them inside the frontier, send them beyond the Yellow River, or break them into small groups. Many were settled in the Ordos, the region inside the great northern bend of the Yellow River. Arrangements changed over time because neither security nor loyalty was guaranteed.

A key tool was the bridle prefecture (jimi zhou). A chief received a Chinese-style office such as prefect. He kept leading his own people, recognized the Tang emperor, and supplied troops when called. Steppe soldiers often fought under their own leaders inside larger Tang armies. Click the dotted term for the definition.

Look at the statue. It is a real Türk-period memorial figure, a reminder that the Türks had their own monuments and their own memory of these years. The next slide lets one of those monuments speak.

Why this matters: this is cooperation at the frontier. It looked expansive on a map, but it was conditional.

Check yourself: What did the Tang gain from a bridle prefecture, and what authority did a local chief keep?

Primary source · a Türk view, carved in 732

“The Turkish lords abandoned their Turkish titles.”

Read closely, on your own:

  1. What did Türk lords give up, and what did they receive, under Tang rule?
  2. Why would leaders of a Türk empire restored after 682 describe the years of Tang rule this way?

Orkhon inscriptions: stone monuments in Mongolia, the earliest long texts in a Turkic language. Fifty years: roughly 630 to 680.

This primary source lets you hear from the other side of the bridle. It comes from a stone monument for the Türk prince Kül Tigin, set up in 732 in the Orkhon valley of Mongolia by a restored Türk empire that had broken free of Tang control in the 680s.

How to read it: the passage looks back on the half-century after 630. Notice the trade it describes: Türk lords gave up Türk titles and took Chinese ones, obeyed the Tang emperor, and fought his wars across Asia. What looked from Chang’an like a successful system of bridle prefectures looks here like humiliation and service to foreigners.

Read it critically: the authors had a political goal. They wanted to warn their own people never again to abandon their own qaghan, so they made the years of Tang rule sound as shameful as possible. That does not make the passage false. It means it is an argument, just like Taizong’s “three mirrors.”

Why this matters: cooperation is not the same as consent. The bridle held while it paid; this inscription shows what some Türks thought of it once they could say so.

Check yourself: How does this inscription change the picture of bridle prefectures you got from the previous slide?

Beyond the steppe · 640–661

Westward, Tang power became a web of garrisons, oasis kings, and titles.

640: Gaochang, an oasis kingdom near Turfan, was conquered and made a Tang prefecture.
648–658: Kucha fell; the Western Türk qaghan was defeated; the Anxi Protectorate moved to Kucha.
Inside the line: prefectures, protectorates, allied kings, and chiefs with titles.
Use the map to locate regions, not to assume equal control inside every line.

Independent study: the western regions, 640–658, and how to read an empire map →

Sources: Cambridge History of China, vol. 3; Shao-yun Yang, Early Tang China and the World.

This slide covers westward expansion briefly; the details are in the independent-study section. Gaochang, an oasis kingdom near Turfan, was conquered in 640 and turned into a directly governed prefecture. Kucha fell in 648 after a campaign that included allied troops. Under Taizong’s son Gaozong, Tang and allied armies defeated the Western Türk ruler in 657, and in 658 the Anxi Protectorate was moved to Kucha. A protectorate was a military command that supervised distant peoples and kings rather than governing them directly.

Read the map. It is a modern map of the empire in 661, at its greatest extent. The darkest area marks the core of direct rule; the lighter areas to the west mark protectorates and looser claims over Central Asia. Even the shading simplifies. Inside the line were ordinary prefectures, protectorates, allied oasis kings, and steppe chiefs holding Tang titles, and control shifted with distance, supply, and the rise of the Tibetan Empire as a rival.

Why this matters: the same bridle logic from the steppe stretched across Central Asia. It looked enormous on a map, and it depended on cooperation everywhere.

Check yourself: What question should you ask before treating any shaded frontier area as ordinary Tang territory?

Place 6 · The Fortress · Ansi, 645

At Ansi, the conqueror won battles but could not take the fortress.

644: Taizong ordered preparations for war on Goguryeo.
Spring 645: Tang armies crossed into Liaodong and took about ten fortresses.
Summer–autumn: Ansi’s defenders held through a long siege.
October: with winter coming and supplies stretched, Taizong retreated.

“If Wei Zheng were alive, he would not have let me make this expedition.”Taizong on the way home, 645 · Zizhi tongjian, ch. 198, translation adapted

Sources: Graff, Medieval Chinese Warfare; Cambridge History of China, vol. 3; Sima Guang, Zizhi tongjian, ch. 198.

×

Goguryeo and Liaodong

Goguryeo was a powerful Korean kingdom whose lands stretched from northern Korea into southern Manchuria. Its capital was near modern Pyongyang. It had already defeated four Sui invasions (see the last lecture).

Liaodong is the region east of the Liao River, in modern northeast China. Goguryeo guarded it with a chain of fortresses; Ansi was one of them.

The sixth place is a fortress, and it is where the conqueror found his limit. Taizong decided on war with Goguryeo and began preparations in 644; the invasion crossed into Liaodong in 645. Click the dotted word for who Goguryeo was. Tang forces captured about ten fortresses and won field battles. Then the campaign stalled at Ansi. Its defenders held through repeated assaults while Tang supply lines lengthened and winter approached. In October Taizong ordered a retreat.

This was not a repeat of the Sui disaster at the Salsu River. The army withdrew in order. But the goal, breaking Goguryeo, was not achieved.

The quotation comes from Sima Guang’s eleventh-century history. On the way home, Taizong regretted the campaign and said that Wei Zheng, had he lived, would have stopped him. He then ordered sacrifices for Wei and had Wei’s fallen memorial stone set up again. The mirror he had lost was the critic who might have saved him from this war.

Look at the image. It is an AI interpretation, not evidence. Defenders line the walls of a hill fortress. Below, the Tang army has pitched its tents, set up two traction trebuchets, and is pushing an earthen ramp up the slope toward the wall. That detail fits the sources: at Ansi the Tang spent about two months building a great earthen mound, and the defenders seized it when part of it collapsed. Now look at the red autumn leaves and the first snow. Season is the point. The Tang army had until winter, and Ansi only had to last that long.

Check yourself: Why is “Taizong lost every battle in Korea” inaccurate, and why is “Taizong conquered Goguryeo” also inaccurate?

Coda · after Taizong, 649–676

Taizong’s son destroyed Goguryeo with Silla’s help, then lost the peace to his ally.

649: Taizong died; his son Gaozong took the throne.
660 and 668: Tang and Silla forces conquered Baekje, then Goguryeo.
670–676: Silla fought Tang attempts to rule the conquered lands.
676: the Tang pulled its Andong Protectorate back to Liaodong.
Victory removed two kingdoms. It did not produce a settlement the ally would accept.

Independent study: the Korean wars, 645–676, step by step →

Sources: Cambridge History of China, vol. 3; Kim Jong-bok, “Liaodong as a Buffer Zone”; Korean History and Culture Committee, A New History of Korea.

This coda carries the story past Taizong’s death in 649 to test the lecture’s thread one last time. His son Gaozong allied with Silla, a kingdom in southeastern Korea. Together they destroyed Baekje, in the southwest, in 660, and in 668 they captured Pyongyang and ended Goguryeo. Tang officials then tried to govern the conquered lands through commands and protectorates. Silla had expected those lands for itself. The former allies fought from 670 to 676, and by 676 the Tang had moved its Andong (“Pacify the East”) Protectorate back to Liaodong. Silla held most of the peninsula south of the Taedong River.

Read the map. Overland, Tang armies had to cross the Liao River and pass Liaodong’s fortified corridor, where Ansi stood. Sea routes could carry troops toward Baekje and Pyongyang. Silla’s base in the southeast made it an essential ally, and later a powerful rival. The arrows are schematic, not exact marching paths.

Why this matters: Tang and Silla agreed on destroying their enemies; they did not agree on who would rule afterward. Victory without cooperation did not last.

Check yourself: What changed between the Tang–Silla alliance of 668 and the Tang–Silla war that followed?

Check yourself · on your own

Why did victory in 630 last longer than victory in 668?

Answer from memory:

  1. Which answer best explains the difference?
    1. The Tang used only diplomacy in 630 and only armies in 668.
    2. The Eastern Türks had no local leaders, while Korea had no allies.
    3. In 630 the Tang entered a steppe collapse and built indirect relationships; after 668 it tried to control lands that Silla also claimed.
    4. The Tang never won a battle in Korea.
  2. How does Taizong’s remark on the road home from Ansi connect the Fortress back to the Mirror?

When you have written your answers, compare them with these possible answers.

×

Possible answers

  1. C. The 630 victory followed a crisis inside the Eastern Türk qaghanate and was turned into titles, resettlement, alliances, and indirect rule. The 668 conquest depended on Silla, whose territorial goals clashed with Tang plans; the allies then fought over the settlement. A falsely separates diplomacy from war; B erases local leaders and allies; D is false, since Tang forces won many battles and helped destroy two kingdoms.
  2. He said Wei Zheng would have stopped the expedition. The critic who served as his “mirror” was gone, and without honest advice he made a costly mistake. He then honored Wei again and restored his memorial stone.

Pause and answer from memory first.

Tips for question 1: go back to the slides on the bridle prefectures and on Korea after Taizong. In both places the Tang won militarily. Ask what happened next: who cooperated afterward, and who did not? The issue is lasting control after victory, not whether the Tang could win battles.

Tips for question 2: look at the “three mirrors” source and the quotation on the Ansi slide together. Notice the memorial stone that was knocked down in 643 and set up again in 645.

Try to use two key words in your answer to question 1: alliance and control.

When you check your answers, look for what you left out and go back to that slide.

Check yourself: State the difference between 630 and 668 in one sentence using both words “alliance” and “control.”

Now step back · what the story shows

Swords won the Tang its empire; cooperation kept it.

Information
registers, the law code, approved texts
→
Resources
grain, cloth, labor, officials, fubing, allied cavalry
→
Relationships
critics, officials, steppe chiefs, allies like Silla

Where it held

Wei Zheng’s court · registered villages · Türk chiefs after 630

Where it failed

Ansi in 645 · Silla after 668 · Türks who broke away in the 680s

Durable rule required cooperation. Institutions made demands repeatable; relationships decided whether people carried them out.

Synthesis of this lecture; see the sources on the preceding slides.

Now that you know the story, you can judge it. This slide states the lecture’s argument.

Information came from household registers, the law code, approved classical texts, and official histories. Resources included grain and cloth taxes, labor, trained officials, fubing rotations, and allied cavalry. Relationships tied the ruler to critical advisers, local elites, steppe chiefs, and allied kingdoms.

The arrows are not a one-way machine. Information was useless if officials could not collect resources, and resources were hard to collect if households hid or fled. Frontier titles worked only while chiefs and their followers found the Tang relationship worth keeping. At court, an emperor needed information only another person could provide, including criticism he did not want to hear.

Look at the two cards. Where cooperation held, the Tang was strong. Where it failed, at Ansi, with Silla, and later with the Türks who broke away, the most powerful army in East Asia could not hold what it had won.

Why this matters: a “strong state” does not mean rulers can do anything. Strength comes from institutions that organize repeated action and from people willing, or compelled, to take part.

Check yourself: Give one example from the lecture for each box: information, resources, and relationships.

Your judgment

What made the early Tang strong: its institutions, its ruler, or its allies?

Institutions

For: registers, land, taxes, fubing, and the code mostly came from the Sui and kept working after Taizong.

Against: they had existed under the Sui too, which collapsed.

The ruler

For: Taizong won the civil wars, kept critics close, and exploited the Türk crisis.

Against: he took power by murder and overreached at Ansi.

Allies

For: steppe allies broke the Türks; Silla made the conquest of 668 possible.

Against: allies had their own goals, as Silla proved after 668.

Pick one, then use the other two to explain where your choice needed help.

Based on the evidence in this lecture.

This is your chance to make an argument. Historians disagree about how much credit Taizong deserves. Traditional Chinese historians made him the model emperor, partly because the histories were shaped by his own court. Modern historians give more weight to inherited Sui institutions, to steppe politics, and to luck.

Institutions: the registers, land rules, taxes, fubing, and law mostly came from the Sui and continued after Taizong died. But the Sui had the same tools and still collapsed, so tools alone do not explain success. The ruler: Taizong won battles, kept Wei Zheng close, and seized the moment on the steppe. But he also killed his brothers and led the failed war at Ansi. Allies: steppe allies helped break the Eastern Türks, and Silla made the conquest of 668 possible. But allies had their own aims, and Silla turned on the Tang.

A strong answer does not say “all three mattered equally.” It picks one and explains how it depended on the others. For example: institutions mattered most, but only a ruler willing to listen could keep them from being pushed past their limits, as Yangdi had done.

Check yourself: Was Taizong more a great ruler or a lucky usurper? Give one piece of evidence for each side, and say which side you find stronger.

Narrative review

Retell the story in nine terms

Gaozu · Taizong

First and second Tang emperors; father and son.

Xuanwu Gate

Site of Li Shimin’s 626 coup against his brothers.

Tang Code

Penal code revised across the seventh century; the earliest complete Chinese code preserved.

Equal-field

Rules assigning use of certain state lands to registered people.

Zu-yong-diao

Grain, labor (or a cloth substitute), and textile obligations.

Fubing

Part-time soldiers in local regiments, concentrated in the northwest.

Heavenly Qaghan

Steppe title Taizong accepted after the 630 victory.

Bridle prefecture

Indirect rule through a local chief holding a Tang office.

Goguryeo · Silla

Kingdom conquered in 668; the ally that then resisted Tang control.

Sources: see the slides where each term first appears.

Use these nine terms to retell the lecture in order rather than memorizing nine definitions. Cover the definitions and try it out loud.

Gaozu founded the Tang, and his son, the future Taizong, won its wars, then seized the succession at Xuanwu Gate. In the Mirror years, the Tang Code gave the empire a legal framework. The equal-field rules linked registered people to land, while zu-yong-diao named their duties in grain, labor or its cloth substitute, and textiles. The fubing system turned selected farmers into part-time soldiers, mostly in the northwest. On the steppe, Taizong became Heavenly Qaghan, and bridle prefectures tied Türk chiefs to the court without replacing their authority. Finally, Goguryeo and Silla show that an ally can help destroy a rival and then reject the victor’s plans.

Study tip: sort the terms by the six places: Saddle, Gate, Bridge, Mirror, Steppe, Fortress. Some places get several terms; the Bridge gets none. Explaining why is a good test of whether you understand the story.

Check yourself: Which term best shows indirect rule, and which best shows the link between households and taxation?

Five-minute writing activity · work on your own

Explain how early Tang institutions supported stability, and where they reached a limit.

How did the Tang structure military service, land and tax obligations, and civil-service recruitment to strengthen the state under rulers such as Taizong?

Write 4–6 sentences. Use one example each for military organization, land/taxation, and official recruitment. Then add one frontier example showing why victory did not always produce lasting control. End by deciding: which connection mattered most, and why?

Adapted from Review Question 2 in the course textbook, ch. 5.

This activity asks you to build an argument from the institutions and then test it against a frontier example. Begin with a clear claim, for example: early Tang stability came from linking registered households and educated officials to repeatable obligations.

For military organization, you might use the fubing system: part-time soldiers trained locally, served capital rotations or temporary campaigns, and went home. For land and taxation, explain how equal-field assignments and household registers supported grain, cloth, and labor obligations. For civil service, describe schools and the mingjing or jinshi examinations while noting that family privilege and recommendations still mattered.

Your frontier example should add a limit, not cancel the first part. You could compare the 630 defeat of the Eastern Türks and the rule through chiefs that followed, or explain how Tang and Silla conquered Goguryeo in 668 but fought over the settlement until 676. Finish by choosing the most important connection. A strong answer does not just say “all were important”; it explains why one made the others possible. For example, registration supplied both revenue and soldiers.

Check yourself: Does your answer include three institutions, one frontier limit, and a final judgment supported by a reason?

Zhaoling · the 650s

The tomb remembered horses and kings. It left out the gate and the fortress.

The horses: six warhorses from the wars that won China.
The kings: under Gaozong, statues of fourteen foreign rulers, from Türk qaghans to Silla’s queen, stood at the tomb’s north gate.
Missing: the brothers at Xuanwu Gate. The bargain at the bridge. The retreat from Ansi.
A monument is an argument. What would you add to Taizong’s tomb?

Previous: The Sui Tragedy (Lecture 1) · Next: the Chang’an elite: the families, learning, and city life of the Tang capital (Lecture 3)

Sources: Zhang Jianlin and Shi Kao, report on the Zhaoling north gate statues and inscribed bases, Beilin jikan (2004); Penn Museum, object C395.

We end where we began, at Taizong’s tomb. Now you know the whole story, so you can see what the tomb chose to say.

The six horses remembered the civil wars: the Saddle. After Taizong died in 649, his son Gaozong added stone statues of fourteen foreign rulers at the tomb’s north gate, among them Türk qaghans, oasis kings, the Tibetan emperor, and the queen of Silla. Archaeologists excavated fragments and inscribed bases in 2002–2003. Those statues remembered the Steppe: Taizong as Heavenly Qaghan, ruler of many peoples. They also exaggerated. Several of those rulers never came to Chang’an, and within twenty years Silla would be fighting the Tang.

What the tomb left out is just as important: the brothers killed at Xuanwu Gate, the payment at the Bian Bridge, the retreat from Ansi, and the critic whose stone Taizong knocked down and raised again. A monument is an argument, like the Kül Tigin inscription and the “three mirrors.”

Next lecture moves inside the capital to the Chang’an elite: the families, learning, and city life of the Tang.

Check yourself: If you could add one scene from this lecture to Taizong’s tomb, which would you choose, and what would it teach a visitor about how the Tang really held power?

Beyond the lecture

Pierian Spring

Optional Independent Study

Eight slides that tell the fuller story behind the lecture’s brief stops: the civil wars, law, examinations, texts, the frontier, the western regions, and Korea.

“A little learning is a dang’rous thing; / Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring.” · Alexander Pope, An Essay on Criticism (1711)

You have reached the end of the main lecture. Everything after this slide is optional, here for you if you want to go deeper or if a brief mention in the lecture left you curious.

The title comes from Greek myth. The Pierian Spring was sacred to the Muses, the goddesses of learning and the arts, and drinking from it was said to bring knowledge. The English poet Alexander Pope used it in a famous couplet: “A little learning is a dang’rous thing; / Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring.” His point was that a shallow taste of a subject can make you overconfident, while deeper study shows how much more there is to know.

What is ahead: eight slides, each linked from a spot in the lecture. They cover how Li Shimin won the civil wars, the Tang Code, schools and examinations, standard texts and official histories, the frontier toolkit, the western regions, how to read an empire map, and the Korean wars step by step. Each slide has a link back to the lecture slide it expands.

Check yourself: Before you go on, which brief mention in the lecture would you most like to understand in detail, and why?

Independent study · The Saddle in detail · 618–628

At Hulao Pass in 621, Li Shimin defeated two rival armies in a single campaign.

620–621: Li Shimin besieged Wang Shichong, who held Luoyang.
Spring 621: Dou Jiande marched from the northeast to rescue Wang.
Hulao Pass: Shimin blocked the pass, waited, then struck. Dou was captured; Wang surrendered.
624–628: southern rivals fell; Liang Shidu, the last holdout, fell in 628.
Force won the battles. Absorbing surrendered soldiers and officials won the country.

← Back to the lecture: consolidation, 618–628

Sources: David A. Graff, Medieval Chinese Warfare, 300–900; Cambridge History of China, vol. 3.

This slide expands the lecture’s quick consolidation timeline. In 618 Gaozu ruled from Chang’an, but rivals held much of the old Sui empire. Two of the strongest were Wang Shichong, who controlled Luoyang, and Dou Jiande, who ruled a large state on the northeastern plain.

From 620 Li Shimin besieged Luoyang. In spring 621 Dou Jiande marched to rescue Wang, hoping to crush the Tang army between them. Li Shimin took a gamble: he left part of his force at Luoyang and blocked Dou at Hulao Pass, a narrow route east of the city. He waited until Dou’s army was tired and disordered, then attacked with his cavalry. Dou was captured. Seeing no rescue coming, Wang surrendered. In one campaign, the Tang removed its two greatest rivals in the east. The fighting near Luoyang is also where Saluzi took the arrow shown on the opening slide.

Look at the image. It is an AI interpretation, not evidence. Tang cavalry with red banners charge down a mountainside into infantry who scatter in clouds of yellow dust, as at Hulao in 621, when Li Shimin’s cavalry broke Dou Jiande’s tired, disordered army.

How it connects: this campaign made Li Shimin the hero of the founding and set up the rivalry that ended at Xuanwu Gate.

Check yourself: Why was defeating Dou Jiande the key to taking Luoyang?

Independent study · Law · 624–653

The Tang Code turned inherited law into a durable framework.

624First Tang code issued under Gaozu, building on Sui law.
637Taizong-era revision reduces some severe penalties.
651–653New version under Gaozong, then an authoritative commentary in 653.
LaterRevisions continue; the transmitted text includes early eighth-century changes.
It is the earliest Chinese penal code preserved in full, not China’s first law code.

← Back to the lecture: laws, examinations, and books

Sources: A. F. P. Hulsewé in Cambridge History of China, vol. 1; Wallace Johnson, trans., The T’ang Code; Shiga Shūzō, “A Basic History of T’ang Legislative Forms.”

This slide expands the “Law” card in the lecture. The Tang Code grew from a long legal tradition. The Sui had already produced a code based on earlier northern models. Gaozu’s government issued a Tang code in 624, and Taizong’s court revised it in 637. Another version was issued under Gaozong in 651–652, followed by an authoritative commentary in 653. The commentary explained how the short legal articles should be understood and applied. Revisions continued, and the complete text passed down to later centuries includes changes from the early eighth century.

That last point keeps the claim accurate. Historians often call the Tang Code of 653 the earliest surviving complete Chinese code. This does not mean earlier dynasties lacked written law; much earlier legal texts survive in fragments, quotations, and excavated documents. The Tang Code became a model for later Chinese dynasties and for law codes in Korea, Japan, and Vietnam.

How it connects: a code made decisions more consistent across distance, part of the “information” that let the court coordinate officials. It also expressed hierarchy: the same act could carry different penalties depending on family and status relationships.

Check yourself: What is the difference between “earliest law code” and “earliest law code preserved in full”?

Independent study · Recruiting officials

Schools and examinations created a route into office, but not an equal one.

Schools: government schools taught the classics to a small pool of candidates, mostly officials’ sons.
Mingjing: close knowledge of the Confucian classics.
Jinshi: literary composition and questions on government; poetry grew more important later in the 600s.
Still: family privilege, recommendations, and connections filled many posts.
Exams widened competition a little. Education and networks stayed unequal.

← Back to the lecture: laws, examinations, and books

Sources: Cambridge History of China, vols. 3 and 5; Chen et al., The Political Economy of China’s Imperial Examination System (Cambridge, 2025).

This slide expands the “Examinations” card. The Tang expanded schools and examinations, but the early system was much smaller and less socially open than the later system you may know from the Song, Ming, or Qing. Government schools prepared sons of officials and some other young men. Candidates could enter categories such as mingjing (“understanding the classics”), which stressed the Confucian classics, and jinshi (“presented scholar”), which tested literary composition and policy knowledge. Poetry became more important to the jinshi examination later in the seventh century.

Passing did not automatically produce an office, and examinations were not the main route for every official. Family privilege, recommendations, school status, military service, and connections remained important. Recent scholarship stresses that early Tang examinations did not destroy the aristocracy; they often helped well-prepared members of elite families rise faster. Still, they gave the court another way to find talent and defined the knowledge officials were expected to share.

Look at the image. It is an AI interpretation, not evidence. Six young candidates in futou caps write with brushes at low desks in a red-columned hall, while an elderly examiner in a red robe watches from a raised desk. Note how few they are. Early Tang candidates were a small, mostly privileged group. Next lecture examines this elite more closely.

Check yourself: Why is “the Tang chose officials by examinations” true but incomplete?

Independent study · Textual government

Standard texts helped officials study, argue, and govern from a shared reference point.

Classics
court-sponsored interpretations of Confucian texts
→
Schools and exams
students prepare from recognized works
→
Official histories
earlier dynasties become lessons for present rule
Standardization reduced disagreement about the base text; it did not end debate about meaning.

← Back to the lecture: laws, examinations, and books

Sources: Cambridge History of China, vol. 3; Howard J. Wechsler, Mirror to the Son of Heaven.

This slide expands the “Texts” card. Government depended on texts as well as taxes. Taizong’s court sponsored a major commentary on the Confucian classics under the scholar Kong Yingda. The project became known as the Correct Meaning of the Five Classics. It drew together earlier interpretations and provided an approved reference for state schools and examinations. It was ordered under Taizong and completed in the following reign. Early Tang scholars also compiled official histories of several recent dynasties, including the Sui.

Standardization did not mean that every scholar agreed or that one book controlled every decision. It meant that students and officials could argue from a recognized textual foundation. The official histories had another political task: they explained why earlier dynasties rose and fell, which made the past useful to present rulers. Taizong’s “three mirrors” saying expresses the same ideal. Remember, too, that the histories written under the Tang shaped how you see Yangdi and how you see Taizong.

How it connects: codes standardized legal categories, registers standardized information about households, and approved texts standardized part of elite learning. All three helped the court coordinate officials far from the emperor.

Check yourself: How did standard texts support both the examination system and the political use of history?

Independent study · A frontier toolkit

Tang rulers used more than one method because frontier problems were not all alike.

Fight: strike an enemy, defend a border, or remove a rival qaghan.
Negotiate: envoys, trade, gifts, hostages, titles, and marriage agreements.
Incorporate: resettle migrants, recruit allied troops, and make chiefs Tang officials.
The same group could be an enemy one decade, an ally the next, and a source of Tang soldiers throughout.

← Back to the lecture: rule through chiefs

Sources: Jonathan Karam Skaff, Sui-Tang China and Its Turko-Mongol Neighbors; Shao-yun Yang, Early Tang China and the World; Palace Museum, Beijing.

This slide expands the bridle-prefecture slide into a full frontier toolkit. Fight includes defense, raids, and large campaigns. Negotiate includes envoys, regulated trade, gifts, titles, hostages, and marriage plans. These exchanges were political: they displayed rank, created obligations, and kept communication open. Incorporate means bringing people into Tang structures without making them identical to registered farming households: resettling groups, recruiting their cavalry, or appointing a chief as a Tang prefect.

Look at the painting. It shows negotiation in action. In 640–641 the Tibetan ruler Songtsen Gampo sent an envoy to ask for a Tang princess as a bride; Princess Wencheng was sent in 641. The scroll is attributed to the Tang court painter Yan Liben, but the surviving version is probably a later copy. It presents the emperor as calm and superior, the envoy as a respectful petitioner. That is how the Tang court wanted the relationship seen.

How it connects: the categories overlap. A victory could lead to negotiation, a defeated people could be resettled and recruited, and an ally could later rebel. The frontier was a field of shifting relationships, not a fixed line between two civilizations.

Check yourself: Which tool would best preserve a local leader’s authority while linking him to the Tang court?

Independent study · The western regions · 640–658

Tang armies and allies opened a chain of influence across the Tarim Basin.

640: Gaochang conquered; a directly governed Tang prefecture set up.
644: Yanqi (Karashahr) attacked after changing allegiance.
648: Kucha defeated with allied help; Tang influence reaches farther west.
657–658: Western Türk qaghan Ashina Helu defeated; Anxi Protectorate moved to Kucha.
A network of prefectures, protectorates, allied rulers, and contested routes, not one block of direct rule.

← Back to the lecture: a web of garrisons, oasis kings, and titles

Sources: Cambridge History of China, vol. 3; Shao-yun Yang, Early Tang China and the World.

This slide expands the lecture’s map slide. The Tang expanded west in stages. Gaochang, an oasis kingdom near Turfan, was conquered in 640 and turned into a directly administered prefecture. Its ruins, in the photograph, still stand in the desert. Yanqi, also called Karashahr, changed its allegiance and was attacked in 644. Kucha fell in 648 after a campaign that included allied forces. Under Taizong’s successor Gaozong, Tang and allied armies defeated the Western Türk ruler Ashina Helu in 657, and the Anxi (“Pacify the West”) Protectorate was moved to Kucha in 658.

Do not imagine the whole area as equally controlled. An ordinary prefecture had a different relationship to the court than a protectorate, an allied oasis king, or a steppe chief holding a Tang title. Garrisons protected routes and projected authority, but distance, supply, local politics, and competition from the Tibetan Empire made control unstable. Even a victory could require repeated campaigning.

How it connects: “expansion” describes several relationships at once, the same bridle logic you saw on the steppe.

Check yourself: Which place on this slide became a directly administered prefecture, and why should you not assume the same status for every other place?

Independent study · Reading an empire map

A single boundary can hide several kinds of Tang authority.

When: the atlas maps boundaries around 700, after the campaigns in this lecture.
Inside the line: Chang’an’s heartland was governed differently from Central Asian protectorates.
Moving parts: Türk, Tibetan, Korean, and oasis powers changed the frontier over time.
Use the map to locate regions, not to assume equal control inside every line.

← Back to the lecture: a web of garrisons, oasis kings, and titles

Source: Herrmann, Historical and Commercial Atlas of China (1935).

This slide teaches a skill: reading an empire map with suspicion. This historical atlas map helps you locate the Tang heartland, Mongolia, the Tarim Basin, and the Korean peninsula, but it needs careful reading. It shows boundaries around 700, about half a century after Taizong’s death. By then the Western Türk qaghanate had been defeated, the Tibetan Empire had become a major rival, and the political map had changed several times. The map also comes from 1935, so its spellings and some interpretations reflect older scholarship.

The most important warning is about the boundary line. Inside it were directly governed prefectures, military protectorates, oasis kingdoms, and steppe communities led by their own chiefs. The court’s ability to collect taxes, appoint officials, and enforce orders differed across those spaces. Some areas accepted Tang titles when the empire was strong and rejected them when another power offered better terms.

How it connects: compare it with the shaded 661 map in the lecture. Maps turn complicated relationships into a clean shape. The shape is an argument. Pair it with the terms “protectorate,” “bridle prefecture,” and “alliance.”

Check yourself: What question should you ask before treating any area inside the line as ordinary Tang territory?

Independent study · The Korean wars, step by step · 645–676

Tang and Silla destroyed two kingdoms, then fought each other over the result.

645: Taizong takes about ten fortresses but fails at Ansi; later raids also fail.
660: Tang–Silla forces conquer Baekje.
668: the alliance takes Pyongyang and ends Goguryeo.
670–676: Silla fights Tang control of the conquered lands; Andong Protectorate moves to Liaodong.
By 676 Silla held most of the peninsula south of the Taedong River; the Tang kept a position in Liaodong.

← Back to the lecture: after Taizong, 649–676

Sources: Graff, Medieval Chinese Warfare; Cambridge History of China, vol. 3; Kim Jong-bok, “Liaodong as a Buffer Zone”; Korean History and Culture Committee, A New History of Korea.

This slide gives the Korean wars in order. In 645 Taizong’s armies crossed into Liaodong, captured about ten fortresses, and won field battles, but Ansi held, and he retreated before winter. Later raids during his lifetime also failed to force a settlement. The official history reports small Tang combat losses but heavy losses of horses; historians treat such figures with caution.

Under Gaozong the balance changed. Tang and Silla destroyed Baekje in 660. In 668 their combined forces captured Pyongyang and ended Goguryeo. Tang officials then tried to govern the conquered lands through commands and protectorates. Silla, expecting gains of its own, fought the Tang from 670 to 676. By 676 the Andong Protectorate had moved from Pyongyang to Liaodong, and Silla controlled most territory south of the Taedong River, with some northwestern areas a shifting buffer.

Look at the mural. It is real Tang art from 706, a generation after these wars. It shows foreign envoys received at court; the figure in the feathered cap is often identified as Korean, though scholars debate exactly which kingdom. It presents envoys as respectful visitors, not as enemies or rivals.

Check yourself: Why did the Tang–Silla alliance fall apart once Goguryeo was gone?
